title: Using `Stream.generate`, produce a fixed number of unique transaction reference numbers for a payment batch. Explain how `Stream.generate` differs from `Stream.iterate`, why it is infinite, and how `limit` bounds it.
shortTitle: Generate a fixed number of unique transaction reference numbers using Stream.generate
keyPoints: Stream.generate(supplier) builds an infinite stream by calling the supplier for each element, ignoring any previous value
Stream.generate(() -> "TXN-" + UUID.randomUUID()).limit(n) yields n unique transaction references
generate has no seed and each element is independent, unlike iterate which derives each value from the previous one
The stream is infinite because the supplier can be called endlessly, so limit is mandatory to bound it
limit short-circuits a lazy infinite stream, calling the supplier exactly n times
generate is unordered, so it parallelizes better than the ordered, dependent iterate
Use generate for independent values like random IDs or constants, and iterate for dependent sequences

s1_definition.oneliner: Stream.generate(supplier) produces an infinite stream by calling the supplier for each element with no dependence on the previous value, so limit(n) bounds it to exactly n values, such as n unique transaction references.
s1_definition.profdef:
Stream.generate builds a stream from a supplier that is called once per element.

- **Stream.generate(supplier)** – each element comes from calling `supplier.get()`, independent of any other element.
- **No seed** – unlike `iterate`, there is no starting value and no dependence on the previous element.
- **Infinite by design** – the supplier can be called forever, so the stream never ends on its own.
- **limit(n)** – a short-circuiting operation that calls the supplier exactly `n` times and then stops.
- **Unordered** – because elements do not depend on order, `generate` parallelizes more easily than `iterate`.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh runs a payment batch and needs a fresh reference number for each transaction. He walks to a ticket machine that prints a new unique ticket every time he presses the button. The machine does not care what the last ticket said; each press is independent. Stream.generate is that ticket machine, able to print forever. Rajesh needs five references for this batch, so he presses the button five times with limit(5) and walks away.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Stream.generate(supplier)

   supplier.get() ─► element 1
   supplier.get() ─► element 2
   supplier.get() ─► element 3
   supplier.get() ─► ...  (never ends on its own)

  add .limit(5)

   get ─► get ─► get ─► get ─► get  ╳ STOP
   (limit stops the source after 5 supplier calls)
```

```text
  generate vs iterate

  generate(supplier)                 iterate(seed, f)
   each element independent            each element from previous
        │                                   │
   ┌────┴────┐                         seed ─► f ─► f ─► f ...
   get  get  get                            (ordered, dependent)
   (unordered)
```

```text
  Transaction reference batch

  () -> "TXN-" + UUID.randomUUID()
        │ limit(5)
        ▼
  TXN-5f2b...
  TXN-a1b2...
  TXN-9988...
  TXN-1357...
  TXN-0a1b...   ◄── 5th call, limit stops here
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
At the National Bank of India, Rajesh runs a payment batch and needs a fresh reference number for every transaction. He uses a ticket machine that prints a new unique ticket on each press, never caring what the previous ticket said. `Stream.generate` is that ticket machine: it calls a supplier for each element, and the supplier produces its value independently, with no seed and no memory of the past.

The stream is infinite because the supplier can be called endlessly. That is safe only because streams are lazy, so the supplier runs only when something downstream asks for another element. When Rajesh adds `limit(5)`, the pipeline calls the supplier exactly five times and stops, giving him a fixed batch of unique references built from UUIDs.

The key contrast with `iterate` is dependence. `generate` elements are independent and unordered, which is why it parallelizes well as long as the supplier is thread-safe. `iterate` elements each depend on the previous one, which makes it ordered, sequential, and the right choice for dates, balances, and counters. Trying to count with `generate` forces an ugly external mutable hack; that job belongs to `iterate`.

The traps are forgetting `limit`, which hangs, returning `null` from the supplier, and sharing a non-thread-safe supplier under `parallel()`. For unique IDs, random samples, and constant fills, `generate` is the clean tool.

Remember one sentence: Stream.generate calls a supplier for each independent element and runs forever, so limit fixes the count, while iterate is for sequences where each value depends on the last.
